The Iran-Iraq War. A brutal eight-year conflict from nineteen eighty to nineteen eighty-eight between the Islamic Republic of Iran under Ayatollah Khomeini and the Iraqi Ba'athist regime of Saddam Hussein. Rooted in territorial disputes, ideological antagonism, and regional power struggles, the war became one of the deadliest conflicts of the late twentieth century, with combined casualties exceeding one million and leaving both nations economically devastated. The conflict drew in superpowers and regional actors, reshaped Middle Eastern geopolitics, and illustrated the limits of conventional warfare in the Cold War era. Iraq initiated the conflict in September nineteen eighty, ostensibly over control of the Shatt al-Arab waterway. Saddam Hussein sought to exploit perceived weakness following Iran's nineteen seventy-nine Islamic Revolution and prevent Iranian expansionism. Iran, isolated internationally and economically weakened by the revolution, unexpectedly repelled Iraqi advances and eventually launched counteroffensives that pushed the war into Iraqi territory, forcing prolonged stalemate. The war featured trench warfare, chemical weapons deployed by Iraq, naval blockade, and "tanker wars" targeting petroleum commerce in the Persian Gulf. Civilian populations suffered tremendously from air raids and artillery bombardment. The Soviet Union supplied weapons and technical support to Iraq. The United States, officially neutral but strategically aligned against Iran, provided intelligence and indirect support to Iraq through intermediaries and allies. The Iran-Contra affair exposed covert U.S. arms sales to Iran, nominally embargoed, while simultaneously supporting Iraq, revealing the complex hidden diplomacy of the conflict. Both nations suffered catastrophic economic losses. Iraq accumulated massive foreign debt. Iran's development stalled and its population endured widespread deprivation and displacement. The conflict ended inconclusively in August nineteen eighty-eight with a UN-brokered ceasefire that restored pre-war borders, leaving neither side victorious but both exhausted. Khomeini's acceptance of the ceasefire was described by him as drinking "a cup of poison."
